clinicalPearls: Placenta praevia is placental implantation over or very close to the internal cervical os, classically presenting as painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy
Digital vaginal examination must be avoided when praevia is suspected because it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage; ultrasound is the diagnostic tool
Many low-lying placentas identified early in pregnancy migrate upward as the lower segment develops, so diagnosis is confirmed on later transvaginal scanning
Risk factors include previous caesarean section, prior praevia, multiparity, advanced maternal age, multiple pregnancy, and assisted conception
Prior caesarean scars raise the risk of associated placenta accreta spectrum, which should be actively sought on imaging
The fetus often lies in an abnormal (transverse or breech) presentation because the placenta occupies the lower segment
Delivery is by caesarean section for significant praevia; timing and setting are planned to allow for major haemorrhage
Management of bleeding episodes includes resuscitation, blood availability, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and anti-D for rhesus-negative women
reference.pathophysiology: In placenta praevia the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment overlying or adjacent to the internal os. As the lower segment stretches and the cervix effaces in later pregnancy and labour, the inelastic placental attachment is disrupted from the underlying decidua, tearing maternal vessels and causing painless bleeding. Because the lower segment contracts poorly after delivery, the placental bed is prone to continued haemorrhage. Prior uterine scarring predisposes to abnormally adherent or invasive placentation (accreta spectrum).
additionalDifferentials: Local causes such as cervical ectropion, polyp, or cervical carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Transabdominal and confirmatory transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta relative to the os
Colour Doppler or MRI to evaluate for placenta accreta spectrum, especially with prior caesarean
Full blood count, group and save or cross-match according to bleeding
Coagulation studies if haemorrhage is significant
Cardiotocography to assess fetal wellbeing during bleeding episodes
redFlags: Heavy or recurrent vaginal bleeding causing maternal haemodynamic instability
Signs of hypovolaemic shock requiring urgent resuscitation and delivery
Imaging features of placenta accreta, increta, or percreta
Non-reassuring fetal heart pattern during a bleed
Bleeding with uterine contractions suggesting onset of labour with praevia
reference.prognosis: With antenatal diagnosis, planned caesarean delivery, and ready access to blood products, maternal and perinatal outcomes are generally good. Uncontrolled haemorrhage, particularly with coexisting accreta spectrum, remains a major cause of maternal morbidity, massive transfusion, and peripartum hysterectomy.
pitfalls: Performing a digital vaginal examination before excluding praevia
Labelling an early low-lying placenta as definitive praevia without rescanning later
Overlooking placenta accreta spectrum in women with previous caesarean and anterior praevia
Underestimating blood loss and failing to prepare adequate transfusion support
Attributing painless antepartum bleeding to a benign local cause without imaging
